reason: Raw type identities cannot be compared across isolated application domains without direct sharing; marshaling a type rebinds it in the receiving domain, so the stated distinction has no standalone C# comparison.
A C# finalizer cannot be named or called; its exclusion from inherited membership has no standalone observation distinct from the base-finalizer execution required by 15.13.
Optional delegate extensions have no required existence, name, signature, or behavior, so no standalone source can distinguish allowed presence from allowed absence.
Optional implementation-specific finalization overrides have no required existence or API, so a standalone program cannot distinguish their permitted absence from their presence.

Once no possible continuation including finalizers can access the instance, its internal inaccessible classification has no C# observer; weak-reference extension APIs add privileged reachability outside this definition.
Collection eligibility is an internal state of an inaccessible instance, and the standard specifies no observable flag or collection deadline by which a standalone program could distinguish it.

Reclamation leaves no reachable instance to inspect, and the standard provides no heap-accounting API or bound on collection time or retained heap capacity from which a finite program could infer freed memory.

The collector's internal usage information and decision process have no C# observer; externally preserved reachability and values cannot distinguish maintained bookkeeping from information reconstructed on demand.

This requirement needs a host unable to supply startup strings with letters in both cases. The pinned Windows .NET host supplies a mixed-case ASCII argument unchanged at ISO-1 and 7.3, so the condition cannot be activated here. Lowercasing inside the program or simulating another host would test that program or simulation. A host with the required limitation and independently established capability is needed; no old-rule conformance, departure or bound is claimed.

Object members are available through interface lookup in both editions, so a successful lookup cannot distinguish the old conceptual member set. Reflection tests a separate metadata model. No isolating common-feature source witness is selected; the old member-set requirement remains explicitly untested.

First-edition 10.1, p. 69, permits additional overloads of Main provided they have more than one parameter or a single parameter other than string[]. A return-type-only alternative such as double Main(string[]) is outside that permission. Under first-edition clause 2, p. 3, a non-syntactic condition without an explicit diagnostic requirement does not provide a deterministic rejection oracle; an ill-formed program can also be accepted after a diagnostic. The test contract cannot require at least one diagnostic independently of acceptance. This predicate therefore has no deterministic reject-or-run test.

ed1-10.4.7-001: The member set is stated without qualification (PDF 87 line 34), invocation is defined with no Invoke member (PDF 157 lines 25-37; PDF 316 lines 25-28), and the edition incorporates only CLI Partition IV, not the Partition II delegate layout that requires Invoke (PDF 19 lines 9-10), so Invoke is not a 1st-edition member. But PDF 17 lines 36-38 let an implementation provide additional methods that change no strictly conforming program, so a compiler that accepts d.Invoke(7) and one that rejects it both conform at ISO-1. No test can expect either outcome; the 7th-edition Invoke rules (E7-4-8-delegate-invoke-method, -return-type, -parameters, -equivalence) belong to a later level and should not run at ISO-1.
A source-level object-member access uses the separate lookup rules and cannot distinguish membership from lookup availability; reflection APIs do not implement the language member-set definition.
